DIY Tractor Repair Runs Afoul Of Copyright Law - NPR

The iconic image of the farmer is someone who works the land, milks cows and is self-reliant enough to fix the tractor. But like a lot of mechanical items, tractors are increasingly run by computer software. Now, farmers are face an obscure provision of copyright law that makes it illegal to repair machinery run by software.

Also shout out to /v/Radio because it's good.

The auto industry has been trying to kill the shadetree mechanic for the past 50 years. Once it finally clicked to them that they could double their income by forcing you to have all of your maintenance done at the dealership, it was only a matter of time before the list of user-serviceable parts (whether through laws or engineering) began to shrink. These days a modern car is absolutely riddled with computers controlling every aspect of its operation and all of the remaining mechanical parts that simply can't be engineered out are hidden under layers of thick plastic shielding and attached with proprietary bolts and there's no service manual available unless you want to buy a subscription to AllData.

30 Years ago you could walk into AutoZone and pick up a Chilton manual for your car, a ratchet set, and a couple of screwdrivers, and basically tear it down to the frame. These days you're lucky if they let you change your own oil and the only reason you have access to your battery is because it's legally required.

Welcome to the future, where you don't own anything that you buy.

Which parts of cars are illegal to work on oneself?

This is just the price we pay for taking advantage of newer technology in vehicles. It gets more and more advanced and the average non-mechanic and non-programmer just aren't going to have the requisite knowledge to safely work on their own vehicles. People would rather have cars that automatically tell them if they have low tire pressure and have computer-controlled engines that maximize fuel efficiency and engine power than having the ability to work on their own cars.

Any attempt to repair, alter or otherwise reverse engineer any of the software stored in your car's computers is a violation of the DMCA. Not so much a big deal for cars as most car owners would rather have a mechanic handle it, but for farmers it's a big deal as they can't often wait for a service person to fly six states over to patch the software on their tractor.
